The ascetic Vālmīki questioned Nārada — the foremost among those devoted to austerity and sacred study, the best of the eloquent, the bull among sages.
"Who in this world today is truly virtuous, and also mighty? Who knows righteousness, and is grateful, truthful in speech, and steadfast in his vows?
Who is endowed with noble character, and who is a benefactor to all creatures? Who is learned, who is capable, and who is ever pleasant to behold?
Who is self-possessed, who has conquered anger? Who is radiant and free from envy? Whom do even the gods fear when his wrath is aroused in battle?
I wish to hear of such a one — my curiosity is boundless. O great seer, you are capable of knowing such a man."
Having heard these words of Vālmīki, Nārada — who has knowledge of the three worlds — addressed him saying "Hear me!" and, delighted, spoke thus:

They rendered due honour to the wise Viśvāmitra, and likewise performed the proper rites of hospitality for the two princes.
Then, having rested for a moment, the two princes — tamers of foes, the delight of the Raghu line — stood with joined palms and spoke to the tiger among sages.
"Enter upon your consecration this very day — may it be well with you, O bull among sages; may this Siddhāśrama be brought to fulfilment, may your word prove true."
Thus addressed, the mighty Viśvāmitra, great sage of brilliant splendour, then entered upon the rite of consecration, self-disciplined and with his senses fully restrained.
The two princes also passed that night with minds well-composed; and rising at the hour of dawn, they paid reverence to Viśvāmitra.
Then those two princes — tamers of foes, knowing the right place and the right time, skilled in fitting speech — spoke these words to Kauśika at the proper place and time.

Then Viśvāmitra, righteous in soul, praised by all the gods and by the seers, the greatly resplendent one, said to the deities: "So be it."
Then all the great-souled gods and the sages, those treasuries of austerity, departed just as they had come, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, O best of men.
Then the great-souled Viśvāmitra, watching those seers depart, spoke to all those forest-dwelling sages, O tiger among men.
"A great obstruction has arisen, stationed in the southern direction; let us set out for another direction — there we shall practise austerity."
"In the vast western region, in the sacred tīrthas of Puṣkara, we shall comfortably practise great austerity — for that is the supreme grove of penance."
Having spoken thus, the greatly resplendent great sage betook himself to Puṣkara and performed fierce, unapproachable austerity, subsisting on roots and fruits.

"Let grace be shown — especially to this king of upright conduct, now wretched, dependent upon you, and with life nearly spent. O queen, O gentle one."
"This was spoken by me in utter desolation, O lovely-hipped one. Show me proper grace — you are, after all, a woman of feeling."
Yet she who harboured a wicked heart, though he was pure of heart — she, merciless, made no reply to her husband even after hearing that wondrous and piteous lamentation of the king, whose eyes were red and brimming with tears.
Then the king, looking once more upon his beloved who was unsatisfied and speaking contrary words regarding the banishment of his son, fell insensible to the ground, stricken with grief.
That sinful woman, gazing upon the descendant of Ikṣvāku — tormented by grief for his son, fallen unconscious to the ground and writhing — spoke thus.

"And Lakṣmaṇa, ever sinless and compassionate toward all beings, serves that great-souled one in the noblest manner — he has gained great good fortune through this."
"Vaidehī, though accustomed to comfort and well aware of the hardships of forest life, follows your son, the soul of righteousness — this too speaks of his greatness."
"The lord who waves as his banner throughout the world the flag that is his very glory, who is devoted to self-restraint, truth, and sacred vows — what has your son not already attained?"
"Knowing Rāma's purity and his supreme greatness, the sun himself surely would not dare to scorch his body with his rays."
"Auspicious at all times, blowing forth from the forest groves, the gentle wind — pleasantly cool, neither too cold nor too warm — will attend upon Rāghava."

Then his fickle mother, in keeping with her own nature as a woman, began to speak of her own deed exactly as it had occurred.
"Rāma has taken no property of any Brāhmaṇa; he has harmed no innocent person, rich or poor; nor does Rāma even glance with his eyes at another man's wife."
"But I, my son, as soon as I heard of Rāma's consecration, asked your father for the kingdom and for Rāma's banishment."
"Your father, abiding by his own nature, did exactly that; and Rāma was sent away along with Saumitri and Sītā."
"That ruler of the earth of great renown, not beholding his beloved son, consumed by grief over his son, attained the five elements — that is, he died."
"Now, O knower of dharma, the kingship must be taken up by you — for it was for your sake that I did all of this."

Rāma, deeply afflicted with grief, placed the piṇyāka paste mixed with jujube and iṅgudi upon a spread of darbha grass, and weeping, spoke these words:
"Eat this with pleasure, O great king — for what we eat is what we offer. Whatever food a man eats, his deities receive that same food."
Then by the same path, ascending from the riverbank, that tiger among men climbed the lovely ridge of the mountain.
Then the lord of the earth, reaching the doorway of the leaf-hut, took both Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa by the hands.
From the sound of those brothers weeping together with the Vaidehī, an echo arose on the mountain, like the roaring of lions.
Understanding the tumultuous sound, Bharata's soldiers were startled and said: "Surely Bharata has met with Rāma" — for that great sound was of those very men lamenting their dead father.

"'How can your brother, now digested by me, have the power to come forth—the demon in the form of a ram who has gone to the abode of Yama?'"
"Then, hearing those words announcing his brother's death, the night-roving demon, in his rage, began to assail the sage."
"He charged at that foremost of twice-born ones, but was utterly consumed by the blazing-glorious sage with a glance like fire, and met his death."
"This is the hermitage of his brother, graced by a lake and forest—he by whose compassion for brāhmaṇas this difficult deed was done."
As Rāma thus narrated, together with the son of Sumitrā, the sun set and the hour of twilight came.
Having observed the western twilight rite with his brother according to the prescribed manner, he entered the hermitage and paid homage to that sage.

"Yet what can I do when you, O wicked one, are like this? I shall go. May it be well with you, O night-wanderer."
That rākṣasa was overjoyed by those words; embracing him tightly, he spoke as follows.
"This speech of yours, full of courage, sounds as if it were said at my own bidding. Now you are truly Mārīca; formerly you were a different night-wanderer."
"Mount quickly this sky-ranging chariot adorned with jewels, yoked with donkeys bearing the faces of piśācas, together with me."
Thereupon Rāvaṇa and Mārīca mounted that chariot, which resembled an aerial vehicle, and departed swiftly from that hermitage-region.
As they traveled they observed towns and forests, mountains and all rivers, kingdoms and cities below.
Arriving at the Daṇḍaka forest, the lord of rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa, together with Mārīca, then saw the hermitage of Rāghava.

Having spoken thus and placed the lord of birds upon the blazing pyre, the righteous-souled Rāma cremated him with grief, as though he were his own kinsman.
Then valiant Rāma, together with Saumitri, went into the forest; after slaying large rohiṇī deer, he spread them out as an offering over the bird.
Taking out the deer-flesh and shaping it into portions, the greatly glorious Rāma offered it to the bird upon a lovely green lawn.
That which the twice-born declare concerning the passage of a mortal soul to heaven — that rite of passage — Rāma quickly recited for his sake.
Then the two sons of that best of men went to the Godāvarī river and both of them offered water oblations to the king of vultures.
That king of vultures, who had performed a glorious and exceedingly difficult deed, who had been felled in battle, who was then consecrated in accordance with the rites fitting a great sage — he attained the pure and auspicious state befitting his own soul.

Hearing the words of the monkey-queen, the monkeys — those shape-shifters — spoke to her in timely and coherent words.
"Live for your son — turn back! Protect your son Aṅgada. Death, having taken the form of Rāma, has slain Vālin and carries him away."
"Vālin, who had hurled uprooted trees and massive boulders — that Vālin has been struck down by arrows like thunderbolts, as if by the thunderbolt itself."
"With this tiger among monkeys slain — he whose splendor was equal to Indra's — this entire army that had charged forward has now scattered and fled."
"Let the city be guarded by the heroes, and let Aṅgada be consecrated as king. Standing firm in his father's place, the monkeys will rally to Vālin's son."
"Or else, O fair-faced one, this stronghold is a fitting refuge for you — the monkeys are quickly entering the fortresses even today."

"There dwells the righteous-souled sage Merusāvarṇi, perfected by his own austerities, renowned, equal to Brahmā himself."
"The great sage Merusāvarṇi, radiant as the sun, must be asked — bowing your heads to the ground — about any tidings concerning the daughter of Mithilā."
"This far the sun illuminates the world of the living, and at the end of night, having dispelled all darkness, sets behind the western mountain."
"Thus far, O foremost of monkeys, it is possible for monkeys to go; beyond this, sunless and boundless, we have no knowledge."
"But having found the princess of Videha and the dwelling of Rāvaṇa, and having reached the western mountain, return when the month is complete."
"No one may remain beyond a month — one who does so shall be condemned to death by me; together with you brave ones my father-in-law shall go."

The sky was filled with bands of great seers, Gandharvas, Nāgas, and Yakṣas; it was clear and pure and wide, frequented by Viśvāvasu.
He moved through the sky traversed by the elephant of the king of gods, along the path of the moon and the sun, the auspicious canopy of the world of the living, spread out and fashioned by Brahmā.
Frequented on all sides by heroes and by noble hosts of Vidyādharas, great clouds blazed as the monkey drew them in his wake.
Darting into masses of clouds and bursting out again and again, he shone like the moon in the rainy season, emerging and entering in turn.
But seeing him flying, a rākṣasī named Siṃhikā, enormous and able to assume any form at will, thought within her mind:
"Today, after a long time, I shall eat my fill; this great creature has come within my power after so long."

He commanded the elephant-footed ones, the dog-footed ones, the cow-footed, and the one with feet small as a talon; the one-eyed one, the one-legged, the broad-footed, and the footless.
He commanded those with exceedingly large heads and necks, those with exceedingly large breasts and bellies, those with exceedingly large mouths and eyes; the long-tongued, the tongueless, the noseless, those with lion-faces, cow-faces, and pig-faces.
"Do whatever must be done, all of you rākṣasīs, gathering quickly, so that Jānakī Sītā swiftly comes under my control."
"Turn Vaidehī around by contrary and favorable means, by conciliation, by gifts, and by the threat of punishment."
Having thus commanded them again and again, the lord of rākṣasas, his soul consumed by passion and fury, threatened Jānakī repeatedly.

With chariots, with frenzied elephants, with horses of great swiftness, with various sharp weapons, and attended by their full forces.
Then those heroes saw the great monkey blazing, rising like the sun with its rays, crowned with the garland of his own radiant beams.
Standing at the gateway — of great speed, great spirit, great strength, great intelligence, great enthusiasm, great body, great might.
Beholding him, all of them took their positions in every direction and attacked from all sides with their respective terrible weapons.
Five iron arrows, keen and white with golden tips, resembling lotus petals, were shot by Durdhara into his head.
Struck in the head by those five arrows, the monkey leaped up roaring into the sky, making the ten directions resound with his cry.

"'I, at least, have reached here—how much more so those of great power? For it is not the foremost who are sent on missions; it is the lesser folk who are sent.'"
"'Therefore, enough of anguish, O goddess; let your anger depart. The leaders of monkey troops will come to Laṅkā in a single leap.'"
"'And those two—like the risen sun and moon—mounted upon my back, those two lion-men will come into your presence, O greatly fortunate one.'"
"'You will swiftly see Rāghava, the slayer of enemies, like a lion, and Lakṣmaṇa with bow in hand, standing at the gates of Laṅkā.'"
"'You will swiftly see the heroes assembled—armed with nails and fangs, with the stride of lions and tigers, those monkeys resembling lords of monkeys.'"
"'You will soon hear the roar of the chiefs of monkeys, resembling mountains and storm-clouds, roaring upon the slopes of Laṅkā's Malaya hills.'"

To the sound of those kettledrums mingled with conches, Rāghava, the mighty-armed Rāma, conqueror of enemy cities, drew near.
Upon hearing that tumult, Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, sat in contemplation for a moment and then looked up at his ministers.
Then the greatly powerful Rāvaṇa, addressing all those ministers there and making the entire assembly resound, spoke thus.
"What you have reported regarding Rāma — the crossing of the ocean, his prowess, and the massing of his forces — I have heard; and I too know you to be those whose valour in battle is true."
Then a rākṣasa of very great wisdom named Mālyavān, the maternal great-grandfather of Rāvaṇa, having heard Rāvaṇa's words, spoke.
"O king, a king who is well trained in the sciences and follows sound statecraft rules his sovereignty long and brings his enemies under control."

That one mounted on a horse with golden and variegated trappings, gleaming like clouds and mountains at twilight, raising a spear bound with rays of light — this apparition moves with the speed of a thunderbolt.
And this illustrious one who comes grasping a sharp trident bright as lightning, swift as the vajra of a servant of death, mounted on a lordly bull gleaming like a mountain — he is Triśirā.
And that one of cloud-like form is Kumbha, with a broad and well-formed chest, collected and steady, with the king of serpents as his emblem, who shines as he draws and brandishes his bow.
And this one who comes bearing a blazing, smoke-trailing iron club adorned with gold and vajra-gems, who stands as the standard of the rākṣasa host — he is Nikumbha, of wondrous and terrible deeds.

Knowing me to be a boy, you should not despise me. Whether boy or elder, know death in this battle."
Hearing Lakṣmaṇa's words, reasoned and of supreme import, Atikāya blazed with fury and took up a supreme arrow.
Then Vidyādharas, Bhūtas, gods, Daityas, great seers, and great-spirited Guhyakas all watched that battle.
Then Atikāya, enraged, strung an arrow to his bow and shot it at Lakṣmaṇa, seeming to compress the very sky.
That sharp arrow like a venomous serpent as it came flying — Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, cut it with a crescent-headed arrow.
Seeing that arrow cut down like a serpent whose hood had been severed, Atikāya, greatly enraged, took up five arrows.
Those arrows the night-ranger shot at Lakṣmaṇa; before they could arrive, the younger brother of Bharata cut them down with sharp arrows.

"Today the king Vaivasvata is even more honoured by me — he by whom you, O mighty-armed one, have today been united with the law of time."
"This is the path of great warriors even among all the hosts of immortals: the man who is slain for his master's sake attains heaven."
"Today all the hosts of gods, the world-guardians, and the sages will sleep in peace and without fear, having seen Indrajit slain."
"Today the three entire worlds and the earth with all its forests, bereft of Indrajit alone, seem void to me."
"Today I shall hear in the inner apartments the wailing of the rākṣasa women, like the trumpeting of a herd of female elephants in a mountain cave."
"O scorcher of foes, the crown-princeship, Laṅkā, the rākṣasas, your mother, me, and your wife — where have you gone, abandoning us all?"

And Rāma, agitated, his eyes burning as if with fire, spoke these reproachful words to the greatly wise Vibhīṣaṇa:
"Why, disregarding me, are these people being harassed by you? Stop this effort — these people are my own people."
"Not houses, not garments, not walls are screens of concealment — the proper veil of a woman is her conduct; such is not the way a woman is honored by a king."
"In times of misfortune, in hardship, in battle, at a svayaṃvara, at a sacrifice, or at a wedding — the sight of a woman is not a fault."
"This Sītā has been through war and has stood in great hardship; there is no fault in seeing her, especially in my presence."
"Therefore bring her swiftly into my presence, O Vibhīṣaṇa — let Sītā see me standing here surrounded by the company of friends."

Thus, O Rāma, those rākṣasas were many times routed in battle by Hari of the lotus eyes, their foremost commanders slain.
Unable to withstand Viṣṇu, tormented by fear, they abandoned Laṅkā and went to dwell in Pātāla together with their wives.
Those renowned for their valour, O joy of the Raghu line, took refuge with the rākṣasa Sumālin and remained in the lineage of Sālakaṭaṅkaṭa.
Those rākṣasas called Paulastyas whom you slew — Sumālin, Mālyavān, Mālin, and those who were their forerunners — all of them, O illustrious one, were mightier than Rāvaṇa.
There is no other slayer of those rākṣasas, even among the gods, O conqueror of citadels, save the god Nārāyaṇa, bearer of conch, discus, and mace.
You yourself are the god Nārāyaṇa, four-armed, eternal — born to slay the rākṣasas, unconquerable, the imperishable Lord.

Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, questioned his ministers: "Where is your king Arjuna today? You ought to tell me quickly."
"I am Rāvaṇa, come here desiring battle with that best of men. You must without delay inform him of my arrival."
Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, those wise ministers replied to the lord of the rākṣasas that the king was not present.
Hearing from the citizens that Arjuna had gone elsewhere, the son of Viśravā turned away and came to the Vindhya mountain, which resembles the Himālaya.
Rāvaṇa beheld the Vindhya mountain — as if filling the sky, as if churning the earth, as if scratching the heavens with its peaks.
Adorned with a thousand peaks, its caverns haunted by lions, it seemed to burst into loud laughter as its cascading cold waterfalls fell.
Where gods, dānavas, gandharvas, hosts of apsarases, kiṃnaras, and their women played together, it towered to a great height, become like heaven itself.

"For the slaying of Lavaṇa in battle, the arrow held by Śatrughna — by whose radiance all you best of gods have been bewildered —"
"— this is the primordial, eternal, radiant arrow of the god who created the worlds, dear ones, by which this fear has come upon you."
"This great arrow was created by that great-souled one for the sake of slaying Kaiṭabha and Madhu — for the destruction of those two Daityas."
"Know this to be the radiant arrow of Viṣṇu; and this Śatrughna is likewise the former body of that great-souled Viṣṇu."
"Go from here and witness the foremost of rākṣasas, Lavaṇa, being slain by the great-souled hero, the younger brother of Rāma."
Hearing those sweet words of the god of gods, they went to the place where Śatrughna and Lavaṇa were both fighting.
All beings saw that arrow, divine in appearance, held in Śatrughna's hand, risen like the conflagration at the end of an age.

(Enter TOXILUS and SAGARISTIO, on different sides..)
TOXILUS:
(to himself.)
He who, falling in love, destitute of means, has first entered upon the paths of love, has in his own labours exceeded all the labours of Hercules. For with the lion, and with the Hydra, with the stag, with the Aetolian boar, with the birds of Stamphalus, with Antaeus, would I rather contend than with love. So wretched am I become with hunting after money to borrow; and yet, those whom I ask know of nothing to answer me, except I have got none.
SAGARISTIO:
(apart.)
The servant that is desirous faithfully to serve his master, i’ troth, it surely does behove him to treasure up full many a thing in his breast which he may think will please his master, both present and abroad.
I neither serve with cheerfulness, nor am I quite to my master’s satisfaction; but, as though from a running eye, my master is still unable to keep his hands off me, in giving me his commands, in making me the support of his affairs.

Have you been quite well all along?
TOXILUS:
Not very.
SAGARISTIO:
I’ faith, it’s with reason then you are so pale.
TOXILUS:
I’ve been wounded in the battles of Venus;
Cupid has pierced my heart with his arrow.
SAGARISTIO:
Do servants then fall in love here?
TOXILUS:
Why, what could I do? Was I to be struggling against the Gods? Was I, like the sons of Titan, to be waging war with the Deities, with whom I am not quite able to cope?
SAGARISTIO:
Do you only take care that catapultae made of elm don’t pierce your sides.
TOXILUS:
In right royal manner I’m celebrating the feast of Freedom.

(to himself.)
The old and ancient calling of my forefathers do I follow, and hold, and cultivate with great care.
For never was there any one of my forefathers, but that by acting the parasite they filled their bellies: my father, grandfather, great-grandfather, great-great-grandfather, his father, and his grandfather, just like mice, always fed on the victuals of others, and in love of good eating no one could excel them.
Hard Heads was their surname. From them have I derived this calling, and the station of my forefathers; nor do I wish myself to turn informer, nor indeed does it become me, without risk of my own, to go seize upon the goods of other people; nor do those persons please who do so; I’m speaking out.
For whoever does this, more for the sake of the public than of his own benefit, my mind can be induced to believe that he is a citizen both faithful and deserving; but if he should not prosecute to conviction the breaker of the laws, let him pay one half of the intended penalty to the public. And let this, too, be written in that law;

Prithee, do give your attention to this. For yesterday I mentioned it to you, and entreated you to lend me six hundred didrachms.
SATURIO:
I recollect it and am aware, both that you did ask me, and that I hadn’t any to lend.
A Parasite’s good for nothing that has got money at home; he has a longing at once to begin upon an entertainment, and to gobble away at his own expense, if he has anything at home. A Parasite ought to be a right down needy Cynic; he ought to have a leather bottle, a strigil, an utensil, a pair of slippers, a cloak, and a purse; and in that a little of the needful, with which he may just cheer up the existence of his own household.
TOXILUS:
I don’t want money now; lend me your daughter.
SATURIO:
By my troth, never to any person whatsoever have I lent her as yet.

Be off and attend to this. (Exit SATURIO.) In the meantime, I want to send a boy to my mistress; that she may be of good courage, and that I shall manage it to-day. I’m talking too much at length.
(Goes into the house.)
(Enter SOPHOCLIDISCA and LEMNISELENE, from the house of DORDALUS.)
SOPHOCLIDISCA:
It were enough to tell an untaught, thoughtless, silly girl the same thing so many times over; really, in fact, I do imagine that I’m quite looked upon by you as a blockhead and a country booby.
Although I do drink wine, still I’m not in the habit of swallowing down your commands together with it. I really had fancied that both myself and my ways had now been sufficiently proved by you; for, as for me, I’ve attended you now these five years; whereas, in that time, a cuckoo even, I do believe, if he had gone to school, could by now have been made to know his letters well; while, in the meantime, whether speaking or not speaking, you have not made yourself acquainted with my disposition.

Then do be off; I’ll off home. Take care and manage this business with attention. Fly post haste.
(Goes into the house.)
PAEGNIUM:
That’s what the ostrich is wont to do in the Circus.
He’s off from here in-doors there. But who’s this woman that’s coming towards me?
SOPHOCLIDISCA:
(advancing.)
Surely this is Paegnium.
PAEGNIUM:
This is Sophoclidisca, the private servant of her to whom I’m sent.
SOPHOCLIDISCA:
(aside.)
There’s not a person this day that’s reported to be more artful than this boy. I’ll accost him.
PAEGNIUM:
At this bar
I must come to a stop.

SOPHOCLIDISCA:
On my honor you shall never this day know before I’ve heard it of you.
PAEGNIUM:
Is such the fact?
SOPHOCLIDISCA:
Is such the fact?
PAEGNIUM:
You are a worthless one.
SOPHOCLIDISCA:
Rogue.
PAEGNIUM:
That befits me.
SOPHOCLIDISCA:
Me then it does not befit.
PAEGNIUM:
What do you say? Are you quite determined, you hussy, to conceal whither you are going?

PAEGNIUM:
Why thither?
SOPHOCLIDISCA:
What’s that to you?
PAEGNIUM:
(standing before her.)
Why, you shan’t go now, unless, in return, I know.
SOPHOCLIDISCA:
You are teazing.
PAEGNIUM:
I choose to.
SOPHOCLIDISCA:
Never, upon my faith, shall you wring this out of me, so as to prove yourself more artful than I am.
PAEGNIUM:
It’s a misery to contend with you in artfulness.
SOPHOCLIDISCA:

Now, to a person that is my friend I shall present these trained oxen from out of my purse; for this, in fact, is a delightful thing, handsomely to bite your thrice-dotted niggardly, antiquated, covetous, spiritless people, who against their servant seal up the saltcellar with the salt. It’s a virtue, when occasion prompts, to hold them in contempt. What will he do to me? He’ll order me to be beaten with stripes, the fetters to be put on. I may get a beating.
Don’t let him fancy that I shall go begging to him. Woe be unto him! Nothing new can now be inflicted upon me but what I have already experienced it. But see, here comes Paegnium, Toxilus’s boy.
(Enter PAEGNIUM, from the house of DORDALUS.)
PAEGNIUM:
(to himself.)
My task that was set me I’ve finished; now I’m hastening home.

PAEGNIUM:
Nothing; for nothing have you.
SAGARISTIO:
May all the Gods and Goddesses confound me, if I don’t this very day, if I lay hold of you, fell you to the ground with blows.
PAEGNIUM:
I am your friend; I trust that what you wish may befall you, and that it may come to pass;
if you fell me, may others make you feel yourself fixed to the cross before long.
SAGARISTIO:
But you may the Gods and Goddesses—You understand what I was going to say after that, if I hadn’t been able to restrain my tongue. Can’t you be off?
PAEGNIUM:
You drive me off with ease; for already my shadow’s getting a whipping in-doors.
(Goes into the house.)
SAGARISTIO:
(to himself.)
May the Gods and Goddesses confound that fellow! just like a crawling serpent he has got a double tongue, and is a wicked one.

TOXILUS:
You speak quite enchantingly; and I shall very soon return you all the money safe;
for now I’ve arranged and put in readiness all my devices, in which way I’m to get this money out of this Procurer.
SAGARISTIO:
So much the better.
TOXILUS:
Both for the damsel to be set at liberty, and, still further, for himself to pay the money. But follow me; I have need of your assistance in this affair.
SAGARISTIO:
Make use of it just as you please.
(They go into the house.)
(Enter SATURIO and his DAUGHTER, in the habit of a PERSIAN.)
SATURIO:
May this same matter turn out well for me, and for yourself, and for my stomach, and for everlasting victuals for it as well for all time to come; that I may have more than enough, a superfluity, and that it may outlast me. Follow me this way, my daughter, with the Gods’ good leave. The matter to which we are to give our attention, you know, you remember, you understand; to you I have communicated all my designs.

DAUGHTER:
Everything.
SATURIO:
Both this, how you were stolen?
DAUGHTER:
I understand it perfectly well.
SATURIO:
